source.title: WorldPM: Scaling Human Preference Modeling
source.authors: Bing Wang; Run-Ji Lin; Ke-Ming Lu; Le Yu; Zhen-Ru Zhang; Fei Huang; Chujie Zheng; K. Dang; Yang Fan; Xing-Zhang Ren; An Yang; Bin-Yuan Hui; Dayiheng Liu; Tao Gui; Qi Zhang; Xuan-Jing Huang; Yu-Gang Jiang; Bo-Wen Yu; Jing-Ren Zhou; Jun-Yang Lin

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Directly investigates whether scaling patterns occur in preference modeling, using held-out Bradley–Terry loss rather than language-model cross-entropy. This is a conceptual test of scaling behavior in a different task and with a different measure.
record.gate_note: The paper reports preference-model test-loss scaling results, which are recorded below. It also reports many preference fine-tuning benchmark comparisons; those are not included as scaling-law rows unless they directly report downstream performance as WorldPM model size or training scale changes. Cited scaling-law results from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study trains Qwen2.5 1.5B–72B models as preference models on up to 15M StackExchange pairs in a single epoch. It reports how held-out Bradley–Terry test loss changes with training data and model size. Preference-model training is a training regime other than next-token pretraining, so this is a new-setting test of V5 (T3). The record's T2 is not quite right: the question differs from the originals' LM cross-entropy, it is not a different method aimed at the same question. The 'power law' is read qualitatively from log2-scale plots; no exponents are fitted. The best-of-N alignment results bear loosely on V6, with the reward model as the scaled system.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors find scaling trends on adversarial sets at all sizes. On objective sets, scaling is 'emergent': only larger models, mainly 72B, show loss decreases across benchmarks. On subjective sets there is no scaling trend, which they attribute to style preferences and annotation subjectivity. They also report that WorldPM initialization improves preference fine-tuning, with larger benefits from larger WorldPM scale.
record.recipe_differences: The original language-model studies measure next-token cross-entropy and vary model size, data, or compute; this paper trains preference models on forum preference pairs and measures held-out Bradley–Terry loss. It examines preference-model size and training-data scale, not compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: Evaluation domain and test set change the scaling result: adversarial tests show power-law loss decreases, objective results vary by model size and benchmark, and subjective results do not decrease with training data. Style control changes subjective evaluations.
record.problems: The scaling results are mainly presented in figures without tabulated test-loss values or reported uncertainty estimates. Trends vary substantially by domain and model size; subjective evaluations are sensitive to style and annotation choices. The paper notes that its preference corpus is approximately 15M pairs (approximately 30G tokens), much smaller than conventional trillion-token pretraining data.
record.rows_left_out: Not applicable; 12 rows recorded. Numerous preference fine-tuning benchmark cells and comparisons in Tables 2–4 and Tables 8–9 are omitted because they compare fine-tuning outcomes with or without WorldPM initialization rather than directly measuring the scaling versions recorded here.

untested.parts: Other modalities (image, video), repeated-data regimes and fitted power-law exponents. Only the preference-model training regime is tested, with qualitative trend descriptions.
Predictability of downstream performance from loss; general downstream tasks beyond best-of-N on Arena Hard and Alpaca Eval.
Not tested: no language-model pretraining loss is measured.
Not tested: no extrapolation from fits.
Not tested: no comparison of fitting choices. Style control as an evaluation choice changes the results (r10), but this concerns evaluation, not fitted exponents.

missing.what: Training loss (single epoch, no reused samples, so effectively held-out) falls logarithmically with data. A sudden drop near 12.6M samples bends the curve away from a smooth trend.
In-distribution validation accuracy improves with both training data and model size.

Safety test-set loss trends differ by size. RewardBench-Safety declines then saturates. RMB-Harmlessness declines at 1.5B, saturates at 7B and ascends at 72B. Pseudo-harmful loss ascends late in training.
Fine-tuning gains grow with WorldPM pretraining scale (72B; 5M/10M/15M checkpoints vs no WorldPM). PPE-objective improves consistently; subjective metrics fluctuate.

record.verdict_notes: There is no fitted exponent, uncertainty, or numeric loss value in the text; every scaling claim is figure-based. All test sets are out-of-domain relative to the StackExchange training data, so the V5 evidence is about transfer of held-out loss. V6 applies only indirectly, because the scaled system is the reward model rather than the evaluated policy.

versions.untested_parts: The study measures preference-model Bradley–Terry test loss, not held-out language-model pretraining cross-entropy as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run fitted loss laws are used to predict the losses of much larger runs.
The study does not compare compute-optimal parameter/token allocations or fit allocation exponents.
It does not compare depth, width, or architecture variants at a fixed parameter count.
Tests preference-model pretraining on text preference pairs; does not test other modalities, repeated data, or whether the same form holds in fine-tuning and transfer.
Downstream evidence is limited to best-of-N alignment evaluations using Arena Hard and Alpaca Eval; it does not establish general downstream predictability across task types.
Does not compare fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits across fitting methods or setups, or test systematic bending away from one power law.

rows.operation_detail: Compared subjective test loss with and without style control.

conditions.value: HelpSteer2, Chatbot Arena, and RMB Helpfulness

rows.baseline: without style control; numeric value not stated
rows.note: HelpSteer2 results are described as stable; Chatbot Arena and GPT4-annotated results show substantial variation. The controlled/uncontrolled gap grows with training data and model size. The authors report that style control makes 72B outperform 7B, while improvement with training scale remains unresolved.
rows.check: This row measures the effect of the style-control evaluation choice. With style control, 72B beats 7B (except slightly on GPT4 annotations), but loss still does not fall with training scale. The model-size effect is partial; the data-scaling effect stays absent.

source_check.correct: For the encoded style-control comparison, versions=[none] and state=cannot_determine: sensitivity to evaluation style control does not establish a power-law scaling effect. Section 3.3.1 separately reports that loss still does not improve with training-data scale after control. Its uncontrolled comparison retains optimized alpha and is distinct from the original raw BT loss.
source_check.locator_found: Section 3.3.1, Figure 4, final results paragraph and footnote on the uncontrolled comparison.
source_check.problem: The partial state conflates a style-control effect and a model-size advantage with partial evidence for V5's power-law form.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5 7B-Instruct evaluated with WorldPM checkpoints
